title: You climb a staircase of n steps, and at each move you take either one step or two steps. Count the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Climbing Stairs (Count Distinct Ways with Steps of One or Two)

s1_definition.profdef: Climbing Stairs counts the distinct ways to reach step n when each move advances one or two steps. The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i minus one plus the ways to reach step i minus two, because the final move is either a single or a double step. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solved bottom-up with two rolling variables in constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India lets a customer clear an instalment plan of n units by paying either one or two units per transaction, and we count how many distinct payment sequences finish the plan.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ways to reach a step equal the ways to the two steps below it, so it is Fibonacci.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Climbing Stairs counts the distinct ways to reach step n when each move advances one or two steps. The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i minus one plus the ways to reach step i minus two, because the final move is either a single or a double step. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solved bottom-up with two rolling variables in constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India lets a customer clear an instalment plan of n units by paying either one or two units per transaction, and we count how many distinct payment sequences finish the plan.

**One line to remember:** Ways to reach a step equal the ways to the two steps below it, so it is Fibonacci.

sections.s2_technical:
The key insight is that the very last move onto step i was either a one-step from step i minus one or a two-step from step i minus two, and those two groups of sequences are completely distinct. So the count at step i is the sum of the counts at the two steps below it. The base cases are one way to stand at step zero (do nothing) and one way to reach step one (a single step). From there we build upward.

The rolling core is `int oneBelow = 1, twoBelow = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int cur = oneBelow + twoBelow; twoBelow = oneBelow; oneBelow = cur; } return oneBelow;`. A concrete check: for n equal to four the counts go 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, so there are five distinct ways. Senior nuance: it is the Fibonacci recurrence with shifted base cases, running in linear time and constant space; if the allowed step sizes were a general set, the recurrence would sum over each allowed step and become the coin-change style count.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers an instalment plan of n units where the customer may pay one or two units per transaction, and the product team wants to know how many distinct payment sequences complete the plan, for modelling customer behaviour. Counting by hand explodes quickly as n grows. This is exactly how Climbing Stairs works: the number of sequences to finish equals the sum of the sequences for the two smaller remaining amounts.

The code defines an `InstalmentPlanService` with `countPaymentSequences(units)` using the rolling recurrence. A `Demo` requests a plan size and logs the count.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a plan of four units. Step 1: we reject negatives and shortcut zero or one unit to a single way. Step 2: we set two-below to one (finishing zero units) and one-below to one (finishing one unit). Step 3: at two units the current is two, so we roll to two-below one and one-below two. Step 4: at three units the current is three, so we roll to two-below two and one-below three. Step 5: at four units the current is five, and after rolling one-below holds five. Step 6: the loop ends and we return five distinct payment sequences, having computed each smaller size exactly once.

```

INFO: Distinct payment sequences for 4 units = 5
Oct 27, 2026 9:34:01 PM com.bank.instalment.InstalmentPlanApplication main
INFO: Final sequence count = 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: units = 4
    │
    ▼
  twoBelow=1, oneBelow=1        (finish 0 and 1 unit)
    │
    ▼ i=2  cur=2 → twoBelow=1, oneBelow=2
    ▼ i=3  cur=3 → twoBelow=2, oneBelow=3
    ▼ i=4  cur=5 → twoBelow=3, oneBelow=5
    │
    ▼
  Output: oneBelow = 5 distinct sequences
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Climbing Stairs is a counting problem that reduces to the Fibonacci recurrence once you see the key insight. To reach step n, the final move was either a single step from step n minus one or a double step from step n minus two, and those two sets of ways are completely separate. Therefore the number of ways to reach step n is simply the sum of the ways to reach the two steps below it, with base cases of one way to stand at the bottom and one way to reach the first step.

Because each count depends only on the two counts immediately below it, I do not need a full array. I keep two rolling variables, compute each step as their sum, and slide the window forward, which gives linear time and constant space. This is the same recurrence as Fibonacci but with shifted base cases, and I always mention that if the allowed step sizes were a general set rather than just one or two, the recurrence would sum over every allowed step size and turn into the coin-change style counting problem.

At the National Bank of India I used this to model an instalment plan where a customer could pay one or two units per transaction, and the product team wanted the number of distinct payment sequences that complete a plan of a given size. I computed it with the two-variable rolling recurrence and cached the results in Redis. Explaining why the last move splits the count into two independent groups, and why that makes it Fibonacci with constant space, is what shows an interviewer I can translate a word problem into a clean dynamic programming recurrence.
